blocks.x: Okay, this is Rio 1 of Don Alba. What's today's day?
Today is September the 18th.
September the 18th, 19th.

Okay, and we're at 910 Royal Street, so we're going to just proceed on. One time you mentioned something to me, and I don't want to mention it by the day, but I thought it was a very interesting point, something that the psychologists talk about. That is, how the guys, some people will change, like they're, with the moon, as the moon changes. Right. And they, what about the man in your band that did that?
Well, that was Geechee Robinson.
Is he a Lava?

I don't know, Dick, but I assume that he is. After he left my band, he went a little while with Fletcher when Fletcher was on the road. He was always a fickle fellow, wanting a gold, gold, gold, so I imagine he just kept running. And I never heard from him, he's one of the characters that never did Carl Strawn much.
Yeah. But what did he do when the moon changed? Can you tell me?

Well, we could, that's what we said, the musicians in the band, we'll joke how it would. Well, he's, his attitude would change, well, we said like a Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde, he'd get off of the beautiful way he lived, and then he'd just pick arguments with anyone in the band. And that's how we knew that we had to stay clear of him a little, anyhow.
Would that be when the moon was full?
Well, we never paid too much.

Well, you know, that is true. A lot of people do change. Like, some people have moods during the course of the day. Right, right, right. Like, some guys get low every afternoon. Have you noticed that?
Right, right. Well, that's the attitude that this fellow had. Yeah. At a certain time of the month, he would just automatically change.
He just, I think we've got the microphone set there. Well, what about most of the guys in the band? How would you compare them, say, as, you know the guys in the Jay McShann band?

Not too well, just a few of them. I remember when the singer Al Hibbler went to Jay McShann. He was probably, all of the guys in there knew me personally. Mm-hmm. But, I've forgotten quite a number of those guys unless they come up and refresh my memory and then I can recognize them.

Well, yeah. Well, the thing I'm getting at, you know, like Lunsford men, they were all gentlemen except Johnny Young said he came up the hard way. Right. And, he was very self-conscious when he went in with the band.
Well, the reason for that is most all of Jim Lunsford's men were college men. Yeah. Or had had some time in college.
Yeah. Well, what about your fellows? How many of them were in college? Do you know?
Not too many, but they were gentlemen.
Yeah. I always get the impression they were very refined fellows.

Well, a very refined group of fellows. I don't think you can find too many like they were today. Well, for instance, I went to school with Cottrell. Mm-hmm. And, we, well, he was a little bit behind me because he's a little younger than I am. Of course, we had Al Freeman, that great pianist. His son is not at the movie store, Al Freeman Jr.
Hmm. I didn't know that.

Yeah. That's his boy. And, well, we had Arthur Durbney and Herb Hall, those are the original members, Alvin Martin. No one with a great education by no reason. But they were very intelligent and very well behaved. Beautiful. Beautiful. Everyone I meet from that band. Well, they didn't, one thing, they didn't drink. I didn't have one in that I could consider a drinker.
Oh, maybe one.
One, yeah. That's the trumpet player.

Yeah. Well, we talked about that, Billy. How about, say, what sort of acts did the guys in the band have? Did they have anything like Lunsford with all the folks? And Lunsford with all the throwing of the instruments in the air. Did you ever do anything like that?

Yeah. Well, Alcorn and I had an act together on that. We had this act together. I'd have Alcorn sit on my lap. He was such a young captain. He was small. And we'd blow the horn. I'd cross. I'd blow. I'd finger his horn. He'd finger mine. A little trick that we thought of meant on there. And we'd throw the instruments in there. And there's some finale. And in those days, standing in the chairs sometime or doing something just to create attention from the audience while you had to do it.
Oh, yeah. They expected you to. They expected you to do that. Did you wave the instruments around ever, doing anything like that? Do which?

Wave the instruments, as you'd say. Oh, yeah. Oh, they would do that. Did all bands do that there? Most all bands in those days. They went through all sorts of motions. All sorts of motions. But nothing, well, I want to say there was nothing pronounced. Yeah. You know, it was just a spodomatic thing now and then.
Mm-hmm. To get back to your very earliest days, we're going to kind of jump around, but... What did you call the neighborhood you lived in? Where you grew up?

The French Quarters. It's all part of the French Quarters. The French Settlement in North Robeson, between Annette and St. Antony. In those days, it was spread out a little more than it is now. Mm-hmm. Go ahead. That's the section there where most of what they said are Creoles were living in. Mm-hmm. And... Bonnie was about a block from me. He was on... he was on Billerish Street. And we all... Manuel Perez was right on Earthquark Street. All of it was concentrated area there.
Mm-hmm. Lots of musicians in. Lots of musicians. Who were some of the other ones that you... What were the other ones that you...

Well, uh... Milford Piron, my teacher. Armand Piron. Thank you. Louis Cottrell's daddy. Bonnie Bigard, the Teos. Lorenzo Junior, Lorenzo Senior. Big I, Louis. Well, we could just go on and name quite a number of them. Piku.
The guys your age, how many of them are there? Let's see.
Well, quite a number of those that I mentioned were just a few years older than me. But the young ones would be like, uh, Cottrell. Bonnie.
Danny Parker lived near you?
Danny was raised with me right... right opposite each other's.
Other side of the street, huh?

Right on the other side of the street. We played in each other's yard. Mm-hmm. When we got mad with each other like kids would do, I'd put him out of my yard today. The next day he'd put me out of his yard. And he'd come back Saturday and Sunday. We were going around together helping his daddy pedal his charcoal and taking care of the horse and wagon. Yeah, Danny's been a beautiful friend of mine. Yeah. For years.
What's pedaling charcoal? I never have seen anybody do that. How they do it.
You've never seen charcoal and stone coal and wood?
I've seen that, but never seen it in New Orleans. I've never seen the way they pedaled it. What did they do?

Well, I don't think you'd see it now. It's such an old page of history. Well, we'd hitch the horse up to the wagon and we'd load the stone coal on the front and maybe the wood on the back or whatever he was going to pedal that thing. He had regular customers who would go to these houses and I, when I was Danny and I would get out and knock on the door and the people would come out and they'd buy whatever they wanted from Chris. That was his daddy, Chris Columbo.
Mm-hmm.

Well, some peddlers used to call out their wares and they'd go through the block and hollering, well, we have, I got shrimp or I got this or I got that. And the customers would come out and purchase it from them. Well, this was a little different with Chris. He was mostly a charcoal or a stone coal or wood pedal. He would pedal.
Well, he never did yell out anything at all.

No, he didn't have to. He had his regular customs. Do you remember some of the things that the other people yelled? Could you imitate them? No, I don't believe I came out. I said, my wife, she said, lady, I got bananas, I got this, and I can't even name it, I got shrimp. And hell, he'd have the shrimp sometime when they'd be watching for the policemen. Policemen come in and he's selling shrimps. He's going to tell it because policemen are going to arrest them because it was a violation of the law to sell shrimps in the open. But they would take a chance.
And that would, I guess they were trying to keep people from getting bad seafood or something.

Right. And that was in the other days, which you can readily see that the way these things sparrow so easily. But these guys could always sell them. And then too, the license, another thing implicated that they were getting by just peddling on their own on these riders.
But they did have licenses.

They should have had licenses then, but not for the open sales when it's like that. So it was a violation, but the guy made his living during that. There's always been violation of the laws down through the years.
What happened on the sidewalks then? You talk about your backyard. Did the kids play on the sidewalks?

Well, the little sidewalks that we had, yes. But mostly we could find ourselves playing in each other's yard. Sometime I'd go to Bonnie's house and we'd play in the backyard band. Next day maybe Bonnie would come to my house, same way with Danny. And then that night we'd go to picture shows, neighborhood theaters. We had the Ivy Theater right down the corner of Hillary. And then that, and we'd find decent pleasurable things to do. Not too much like, of course I don't want to condemn the error because in so doing and you don't accept progress. But I do believe that kids were more beautiful in those days as far as being obedient to the parents and also to the elders. They respected another person just as much as they respected their own parents. And a lot of times we find ourselves getting a whipping for something we've done maybe from the next door neighbor. And we better not tell our parents because we would get another beating after that. So all in all the kids were, well maybe it's because there weren't so many like it is today. It's such a big thing. I don't know how you can control it. In those days it was more easily controlled.
Well I don't think all change is progress. I mean there's such a thing as progress and there's such a thing as just plain change. Something's good and something's bad.

But you don't retard progress. But in so doing you've got to have, you have to have a borderline on what's right and what's wrong. And that's what we're going to have today. The borderline has been forgotten. That is my way of thinking. Somebody else may have a different eye.
Well I think there's so many kids now and you can't say anything about kids in general. You have to talk about different kids. I find different kinds of kids.
That is correct.
And I deal with all the time. Some are very smart and some are good and some are bad.

Yeah but the main thing is this, they don't want to be controlled. They don't want all the person to say anything to them. Because the first thing that strikes you with is this, you're old time. You can't tell me what to do. Well, maybe so. That might be right in that way of thinking. But I always say this, that the Ten Commandments is a guideline for anyone to go by. But then they'll tell you who wrote the Ten Commandments. There's always a question in their mind that you're telling them. And it's a matter of trying to confuse you so that you don't know what to say. But you have to be prepared to answer any questions that they're asking. And getting back, I still believe that the kids in the days when I was small were more subdued. And they had a little bit of more control over their thoughts and the things that they did. They've tried to follow into the instructions of the elders that could give them that necessary experience.
Do you think they were happier then?

I think they were. Nobody ever, we never dreamed of shooting or cuttings or things like that. When something like that would happen, why, it was a big headline. Today the whole paper has it. Not only one article.
You might have had a few fist fights.

Oh, we had fist fights. Dan and I had many fist fights. We'd fight over a baseball bat, over a baseball glove or something like that. And Bonnie and I used to fight like two strange dogs. Today and tomorrow we'd be hugging and kissing each other. But it wasn't serious fights.

Well, your family, that's one thing I noticed yesterday. We were at the concert and families are very affectionate, you know. People, the Creole families, you know, they hug and kiss each other and they're always glad to see each other. And people always shaking hands and touching each other.

It's been a trade. It's always been a trade of the Creole people to hug and kiss each other whenever we met. And like Joe Marius told my sister that he has never seen any family as crazy about their relatives as we are. Because my sister sold over 200 and some tickets.
Oh, I can't believe that. She told me she sold over 100 when I was talking to her trying to get that.
Yeah, well Jill brought us some more tickets.
Anyway, you mentioned ball. That just happened was one of the things I was going to talk to you about. Did the kids play ball much then?

Oh, we had ours. We used to make our balls. We used to take a stocking and rip it and just wrap it up and make a ball. We probably, sometime we put a little, a little, uh, small ball, a wooden ball or something, and then we'd wrap this thread around this ball and then sew it to keep it from, from threading. We had a way of sewing the ball. And we'd play until it would rip up and then we'd make another one. That was our balls. We didn't have any good balls or good bats. We had handy downs. Sometime a kid was able to, uh, to come up and get him something new. He might have worked around and made a few nickels and finally would buy him something. We all would use it.
They'd have little jobs, huh?

Little jobs. Well, such as when I was a kid, I, I shined the brass faucets for nickel and I would shop for the neighbors and get 50 cents a week and go get all that grocery. I guess that's why I know how to cook and shop today. Because it was, I'd go for four or five of them. And of course, there was a lot of other ways, shining shoes and, uh, working in the baker shops and cleaning up this and that. If a kid really wanted to, to get along, which they did. There was a lot of little jobs. They weren't lazy. We got out and did our chores. Went to school. Sometime we had a nickel to go to school. That was our lunch. Mm-hmm. Sometime the kids, one kid would buy a pickle with his nickel and another kid would buy a piece of bread with his nickel and maybe another one would buy some. Meats were so cheap, they didn't get four or five slices of ham or sausage. And you'd have enough for you to chip in and split and go and make your sandwiches.
Mm-hmm. What kind of, uh, ball games did you play? They must have been not just baseball.

No, well, we had stick ball. You had stick ball. Stick ball. You hit, you hit your stick, your baseball bat might have been an old broom handle. Mm-hmm. Hit the ball, you run the first base, you had first, second and third base. Then sometimes as the, as the times went by, we would go out into the greens, which we used to call back of town. Back of town, back around St. Norton and Johnson, all those were big green lights. Mm-hmm. And a lot of the, a lot of the old baseball players, the Ray Bolton baseball players, before the Crescent Stalk Park was put up, they would play on the greens with the kids.
Mm-hmm. They, they got a kick out of them.

That's right. One of the real great pitches they had, it was a fella named Joe Pato. And, Pato, I think it's a P-E-R-D-O, I'm sure that's how you spell it. The old Thomas would remember that name. Mm-hmm. He, he would stop and, and play baseball with the kids, and with this old rag ball, and then leave them, go to Crescent Stalk Park, and pitch 18 innings against the great, great ball players. Mm-hmm. Buck Leonard, and, and, and, and, to name a few. Yeah. He'd be right in there, pitch 18 innings.
Do you remember, you said the Crescent Starks?
Crescent Starks? Crescent Starks. Crescent Starks. Well, it was a Crescent Starks team, two years.
Yeah. And the Blank Pelicans, do you remember them?
That's right.
LGS Giants?

Well, those are the baseball teams in the days that I'm talking about. They're both Crescent Starks Park, and that's where the main, uh, baseball games were played, even when they brought the, uh, the big stars down, like the Chicago Giants. And, of course, they picked up a few of the ball players from around here. Jumbo Jackson was one. And, uh, Satchel Page was down here. He's pitched down here. And the great catcher, Josh Gibson, and all the guys that they're naming today, which is, uh, late in life they've named these great people. But it is great to know that, uh, now that they are being remembered for the, uh, part that they're played in these United States. And, uh, when they, some of the commentators mentioned, uh, the greatest baseball pitcher ever lived in, and he named Satchel right, he's really correct. There's a guy, a guy that's done some great feats on the diamonds that no other man has accomplished. And Dizzy Dean and, and, uh, Bob Phillip, they bond stormed with, uh, with Satch. And a lot of times, nine times out of ten, he was on the winning side. Of course, these things are kept in the dark. Yeah. They're kept in the dark. It takes away too much from Dean and Fav. Uh, those other great pictures that he pitched in this. But, uh, to them, the records, if you dig, dial it into it, you'll find the records of that. Same with you great musicians, uh, there's one fella that I think I mentioned to you once before, Placy, uh, not Placy, but Caffer, Darren's player, but Placy was the brother. Uh, Caffer was a genius. Not just a musician, a genius. Uh, it's too bad that some of his, uh, artistry isn't, hasn't been captured. I think one, uh, one record that you asked me about, that's him actually on this record playing this mandolin. Yeah.
You said you were in the studio, you told him. Right.

You were there, of course. Well, it's a banjo, uh, like, and, of course, you had another great one, but I don't think he was quite as great as Caffer. It was John, John Morello. Well, he was, he was tremendous. Then, all right, then you go down into, uh, to the clarinets like Lorenzo T.O. Jr. Uh, and the old man, uh, we called him Papai. Uh, huh. That taught all of us how he's a symphony man. Uh, huh. Those guys read music just like the newspaper. I imagine that. I was talking to my professors' daughters last night, Milford P. Romwe used to call him, in other words in English, it's Milford.
Uh, huh.

And the guy could, uh, do everything on the trumpet, but play jazz. He was quickly a symphony man, triple tongue, double tongue, and read music. In fact, the old, the old musicians used to get together at the Autocrat Club on Sundays, and they'd have about 25 to 30 playing all these high-powered, uh, symphony notes.
And you'd listen to that, too?
Did I what?
You listened to that.
Oh, sure. I was a kid, I used to sing. Yeah. They'd put me on as a singer.
What did you sing with them?

Uh, little, little bitties like, uh, Roses and Biggity, which was in them days, like that. I'd pick out, they'd pick out something simple, you know. Mm-hmm. Just, uh, to promote friendship and feelings like that for the audience, and with, uh, mostly family. Yeah. Wasn't to the public.
Yeah, it was a neighborhood affair with families. Right.
With the, uh, Autocrat Club behind it. Yeah, I see. Yeah, I see. Yeah.
Do you remember any of the pieces that the symphony band, the symphony orchestra?
No, no. I can't remember. Yeah, yeah. I can't remember them now. They could spend two or two for a while. Oh, yeah.
Yeah. It's like, you know, who knows how old Satchel Paige is. Right. You know, I mean, could you guess?

Well, you make a guess. Uh, Satch and I used to, uh, pal around together. Uh, one time in Dallas, he felt like riding. He used to like to ride and he plays a guitar. He sat on the back of the car and ride. We never discuss Edge. I don't know why. But I do know this, that he's, he's older than me. And I was 64 years old in August. So I'm not gonna question Satchel's age. He's a little older than you. Yeah, if he says he's 29, that's his business, you know. Yeah.
No, I think he came out, I saw him on This Is Your Life, and he came out with his age.
Well, that's problematical too, because I saw the program and I don't think it was a definite answer. Yeah.
Well, maybe he didn't know, because they didn't keep records. Possibly so.
Possibly. Possibly.
What did he play on the guitar?

Just play the blues and sing blues. Just simple chords. You know a lot of guys do this as a pastime, but sometimes you run into a fella who does it as a pastime, really gets some good music out of what he's doing. Uh huh.
It's great. Yeah, some guys can only play three chords, but what they do in three chords is great.
That's right.
And to me, they're real musicians in that, in their limit, you know, you have to give them

a lot of credit. They're real artists, but limited. Well, sure. But he's never had a lesson in his life. What he's doing, he's just picked it up and went ahead. Well, so many musicians in the old days did that. And even today, even today, these young guys that are playing these guitars, they don't know music. They're listening to a record, they're learning this instrument some kind of way. I can't explain it how to do it, but they go right ahead and they make the correct changes and chords and play exactly what the other fellas play.
They're getting the correct changes.
Yeah. So we had a great guitarist in Willis, Santiago.
Let me move all this stuff and get it out of your way.
Willis, Santiago, I'm doubt seriously, was what we would call a great musician before. He was an artist. Yeah. He was a great artist.
Well, what made somebody like him great?
Well, I guess you'd call it natural ability. A guy's just born with a natural gift.
Could he play fast or did he? Play anything.

He's played old Tom Anderson's cafe up here where Cress is up on. Yeah. And that was days when Bonnie was with a real young fella, Paul Byrd, and they had a tremendous little band there. And that's where Bonnie and Alvin Nicholas left and went up to Chicago to join. King Oliver.

Well, it strikes me, you know, when I talk to New Orleans musicians, I never know exactly when they say somebody's great, exactly what the man was great at. Some guys are great at, say, you take Caffrey Dyer and Jerry. I don't know if he was great at keeping a beat with the correct chord changes.

No, he was great in everything. He could solo, he could chord, and he could improvise his own ideas. Which, all in all, that's what you say when you say a man is great. Yeah, all in all. All in all. Now you might have some musician that's great in soloing only. Yeah. But as far as being able to tie himself in with the other musicians, no. Yeah. Well, that fella, you can't consider him as great. Mm-hmm. Because he's confined to one thing only. Yeah.
Well, some people are great readers but can't play, you know. That's true.

Yeah. A lot of, well, for instance, for a long time, when I was with Troy First, joined Troy Floyd's band, I didn't have too much time for solo work. Yeah. Most of mine was reading because the fellas in the band were limited. And of course, naturally, I had to play three, four, five different parts. Yeah. But as the band got older and we got to playing together, well then I could occasionally get out and solo.
Mm-hmm. Well, you must have been an awful good soloist, changing from the rapids. There's so many things.

Well, the training that I had is responsible for it. Well, for instance, my daddy was a musician and in fact, most of my family were musicians. But staying right there with Manuel Perez, Milford Piron, old man Gus Moret, and people like that, and you have to learn, otherwise you don't have nothing in your head if you can't learn with these fellas. George Moret. Old man George Moret. Yeah.
Did he actually teach you?
No, but we were almost like relatives. I'd be at his house all the time. Yeah.
I see.
He went to... Old man George didn't have too much time for teaching.
Well, I imagine he was busy with his band.

Always busy. Always busy. And I had one of the musicians in my band as a product of those old bands, one of my first bands, that was old Jimmy Johnson. See, Jimmy played with Buddy Bowling and those guys.
Did he read much or was he fake?
No, he could read. No. But here's another case of a gifted musician. Even his tonation on the bass. It sounds strange to say a man gets a different tone out of a bass but that's certain.
Oh yeah, sure.

You take like Blanton that was with Duke that died so young, well Blanton could make his bass sound like a shallow. And those are the things that a lot of musicians don't know how to get tonations out of their horns. You know the smart playing. It's not what we call a pinch tone, it's a round tone, it's big. And a lot of musicians in those days, the first thing they did, they studied their tonations. Like Big Al Loy, Lil Nelson, beautiful tone. Piku, tonation. Or listen to Bonnie's tone.
Well a lot of guys had to work in the street and I think that you have to develop strength and tone and everything there.

So I was, I meant to ask you something Dick. Frank Driggs wrote and told me something and he says, well I have a different story from you than what Dick Allen says. I said, man I'd like to know what it is. He said, because everything I've told Dick is from my own chops.
Yeah, well.
I was wondering what it was, he never did tell me.
No, no, well there's a lot of different things.
Now maybe he was talking about something might have happened in Texas and we might have confused me. So that's something happened here.

Well of course, it's easy to get two sides of the same story. I mean if one man tells it one way and another one tells it that way. But both the truth is each man sees it. Right. He never did. Oh, back to the kids games. Did you ever play hopscotch?
Yeah, sure. That was with the gals. The gals played hopscotch. Yeah, right. We'd draw the hopscotch for them on the sidewalk.
So you had little girlfriends around there. Oh yeah, sure. And they'd do all that kind of stuff.
Yeah, hopscotch was that game. Yeah. And hide and seek, you'd run and hide and then you'd hit a can and say one, two, three, I spy so and so and you'd have to tell them where you're spying.
And he's it.
The guy who's it hits a can. Right.
Did you ever hear the game of Rockette? That might be from before your time.
Maybe we're not saying the right word to Rockette.

No, Rockette. Rockette. They had a Rockette field back on Allegiant Field Avenue. No, I don't think so. I used to hear about it I think from guys back in the 1890s. But the game died. It was like lacrosse. Yeah, no.
I never knew it.
I think it must have been an Indian game that got brought to New Orleans. Right. Oh, you mentioned the movies then. They were silent when you were young?
That's right. Silent creatures.
Well, what kind of noise did they have? Did they have anything?
Well, there wasn't any noise. None at all. Look at the thing there, turning over the film. Didn't have any piano player?
Sometimes, yeah.
Sometimes they had a piano player in the pit.
Anything more than a piano player?
Well, I remember the time his theater way up on Washington. I can't remember the name, but I played in the pit with an old guy named Tolles. He was a bass player.
Oh, yeah. Not Tolles' daddy properly, huh? It was not himself.
Oh, not.
Not Tolles, huh?

Yeah. And he played in the pit during the intermission. Then the pitch would come back on and the band just started to play again. A lot of times in the... Well, that's why Eddie Hewitt's daddy was in Atlanta, Georgia, a pit piano player. Oh, the tape's about to run out. Let me get a little... Is that up?
I hate to get in the middle of anything. You got plenty of time? You got plenty of time?
We're talking about the different movie pianists. Do you remember any others?
Well, right offhand, no, I sure don't.
You say Tolls played bass? It was bass player. And you were playing trumpet?
I was just a kid then. Oh, just about six, seven, eight pieces. The regular bands like they had around here.
Did you ever hear of anything like that? Is there a Railroad Avenue in New Orleans?
Railroad Avenue?
Yeah. You go to all these little towns that have a Railroad Avenue.
Right, I never heard of it. The other side of the track.
There's no such thing as the other side of the tracks in New Orleans.
In those days it weren't. I can't remember it being. Well, in other words, you're trying to see a segregating place as such as the other cities. No, yeah.
I don't remember New Orleans as ever having any slimes until the government made it.
Well, no, like I say, people lived all over the city of New Orleans. I guess that's because of the melting pot that's been here.
Yeah, it always strikes me that every neighborhood had its own character. Right. A lot of people owned their own homes.

I don't know about owning a home so much in the old days. Everybody would rent as well. For instance, this house where I was born, my brother lives in it now. It's just been handed down from my daddy to him. And they don't own the first nail any. They're still paying rent. But like today, it's a different day and time. And people are owning their own homes now.

That's not. Mm-hmm. All right. I was wondering, let's see another thing. Back to your big band days. Do you remember Kiladillas? Did you ever use that expression or tune? Yeah. What was a Kiladilla? That meant it was the best thing you were going to play and you were going to knock the audience out with that one. That's a Kiladilla. That was your ace in the hole. Would it be a slow number or a fair number?
No.
No. No.
No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No.
No.
No. It was probably something that everybody could blow on.
It was a real swinging number then. A real swinging number.
That's a Kiladilla.
And it would feature everybody in the hole?
Most everybody could feature the show. Yeah.
What about riffs? Did you have any riffs numbers in there?

Set your own riffs. One would follow the other. Yeah. As of guys making a solo, you set your riffs on the end. Mm-hmm. Stay in the chord formation. There's something to back him up from that, just being out there swimming by himself.
Well, my rocking and swinging, I think about that. That's nearly all riffs except for the solo.
Mostly. Mostly. How many numbers did you... The big thing was the rhythm section on your rocking and swinging.
How many numbers would you have like that, would just be based on a riff?
Quite a number of them. Quite a number. All during the night. You bring one in on a set. I'd play a set of three numbers and your killer diller would be your third number.
What bands were famous for their riffs then?

Well, most all bands. All of them set their riffs. The Blue Devils, which was Ben and Morton's band, great riff band. And of course, from there came the Count Basie band. And you had Lansford, my band, Andy Craig, T Holder, Troy Floyd, Trent. Now Trent was a little more sophisticated band, something on the P-Rong style band. Played mostly the high class hotels and schools and colleges in those days. But they also played a lot of gigs, outside gigs. It was one of these real fine, classy bands, Trent was. Troy was also, but not... To me, Trent was a more refined band, if I have to say it myself. The thing about Troy Floyd's band, were the instruments, everyone had beautiful instruments. It was called the Orchestra of Gold. And in those days, I didn't have to buy my instruments. C.G. Khan gave me my instruments and used my picture in the little folders to advertise me playing a C.G. Khan trumpet. I wish I could find some of these old memoirs, but I just can't find them.
I know some of the guys that work for C.G. Khan, and maybe we should ask them.

I believe it's a long shot. You'd have to go way back to where the original office was in those days, which I can't recall. And they possibly might have something on the shelf. It goes way back to 26 and 27.
What do you think has lived? What do you think you've done among the numbers with your bands? Say tunes. How many of them are still played today?

Most all of them are still played. Because all of them were mostly copyrighted numbers, except some of the numbers that we call hidden numbers. They're just some of the guys thought up in the band. And when hidden didn't register them as copyrighted numbers. But any of the older bands, any of the old musicians, they still play all those numbers. They're standard numbers as far as...
I think True is certainly a standard. I mean, not just...

Well, it isn't a standard, Dick. It has never been put on the market as a number. It could have gotten to be a big thing when Paul Gaten put it on. Yeah. But, so the company wouldn't pay us off, the writers. You see, Paul Gaten put this on the black market. He said he had written a song in the Scotchrell and I. And, uh, Linden, New Jersey is where the record company was. They lined up the records to not pay us.
Well, you know, to me, that's a standard because people still play it today.
Well, here. Here in New Orleans.
Yeah, in New Orleans.
But not after you leave here.
Oh, it's not popular.
No, it isn't. I wish it was. Yeah.
Well, what about the Sheik of Araby? How many bands play that like you here? None.

A lot of them copied after the little diddy that we put in. But the Sheik of Araby is just another, another blind number, in other words. You can roll that number and riff on it and other guys can riff on it.
They still sing that. They still do.
It's a little catchy diddy. Yeah. In those days it was something obnoxious. Today it's too subdued. Yeah. To sing with no pants.
Right. Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah. Uh. How many tunes did you write that you know of?
My self-pustion was about another five or six.
The names of any of them?

Well, Latru was about the only one that I can remember. Right here and now. And there was one, Alita. Never did too much. It was a beautiful song. Phil Tiller was my alto player. Between me and I we got this Alita.
It's called what?
Alita. A-L-I-A-L-I-T-A. A-L-I-T-A.
A-L-I-T-A.
Alita.
Alita. What about guys then when they played solos? Would they be based on chords or scales or would they make up new melodies or what would

the idea be? You mean their own individual solos? Yeah. It was the way he felt for his improvisation. Well, I'm sure. Of course, he has to stay in the area of the chord formations of the song. For instance, he plays a 32-ball chorus. He has a different pattern than if he's playing a 12-ball blues.
Yeah.
So his ideas have to change to what he's playing.
Well, how many of them run chromatic scales a lot? Who do you think of it?
Most any good musician. He doesn't run a chromatic scale. He's playing. He runs a chromatic scale maybe when he's tuning his horn up and running from the bottom to the top.
Well, sometimes in a solo you'll hear a guy use some chromatics.

Yeah, chromatics. Yeah, chromatics. Which is different from a chromatic scale. Yeah. See, a chromatic scale is just a scale of the notes. So if he's making chromatics, he's making a different chord formation into his brain.
Yeah, I'm telling you, Cattro didn't use a lot of chromatics.
He does.
He does.

Well, I think Cattro has to be rated with the... With all the great clarinet players. He has to have a spot there. Because there's no doubt about it. His tonation, his improvisation, and his sense of the song that he's playing, it's all bad. And what about...
What were your exercise books that you had? Well, I had a French book that someone stole from.

It was called the Clodermier. C-L-O-U-D-M-I-E-R. It's the old French method. And it had everything in it. It had, from the beginning, the whole notes, then the half notes, then the quarter notes, and so forth and so on. And there were a lot of solos in there that were taken from Poet and Peasant and these other things like that. But this book was stolen from me and I've never been able to get another one like it. And just like my Sol Fage book that I learned to sing the notes and the music too, those were stolen from me. And I've never been able to get another one like it. And I was thinking about going into the loft of that old house up there and see if the rats have them beaten up and everything. I'll tell you, I might run across one up there. What Sol Fage book did you in? But this book was stolen from me and I've never been able to get another one like it. And just like my Sol Feds book that I learned to sing the notes and the music too, those books are gone and you can't find them. I was thinking about going into the loft of that old house up there, see if the rats had them heating up and everything up there. I might run across one up there.
What Sol Feds book did you use?
I can't think of the name of it. All this was old French methods.
A lot of people use Italian Sol Feds.

Yeah, over here. Pascal Bono. Right, right. They all are basically the same. In fact, it is basically the same. Now that the print might be a little different. Or maybe some of the notes might, I mean, the formation of the notes might look a little different. But basically it is the Sol Feds is the same way anywhere you're going. It's the beginning of music, what music is. And a lot of these fellas there, you tell them Sol Feds, they don't know what you're talking about. You ask them what is music, they can't answer you. Because they don't know. And when you tell a guy, music is a combination of sounds that are pleasing to the ear.
Yeah.

Then he couldn't explain it to you because here's a damn show not pleasing to the ear. When he's going to play all these loud noises on the guitars and on that electric bass, then it ceases to become music. Yeah.

What about something like where you'd have the piano, I think about Sunny Side of the Street. The piano player is playing the melody, playing his part, and the saxes are playing a background. Do you remember that, your record? Do you remember that part now? It's probably been a long time since you heard it.
In which number?
Sunny Side of the Street.
Oh, that was the one that Billy Douglas sung and played the trumpet.
Yeah, but there's a little piano part in there.
Oh, yes, an interlude.
Yeah, a little interlude.
There's an interlude and he brought Billy Douglas in there. No, Dink Taylor came after the interlude, if I remember.
I forget.
Yes, that was a written arrangement.
But to me, I never hear many records where the piano stands out over the saxophones. You know, with the saxes in the background. Well, that was a very unusual thing.
It was. It was Lloyd Glenn's idea himself.
Oh, I see. You would work it out together.
Right.
Once you arranged it.
Right.
How often did you rehearse?
Dink, we actually rehearsed most every day.
And you were traveling?

We were traveling. We would get into a town early and maybe rest a little while and I would call a rehearsal. And then, of course, the guys would tell me, say, old man, call a rehearsal. We got a new arrangement to be back together. Well, no problem. Nobody late. Nobody grouchy.
Yeah.
Come and rehearse. And sit down and do what you had to do and leave.
What about microphones?

No microphones. We used to use the old megaphones. Sing through the megaphone. This old long horn looking thing. Oh, yeah. Wasn't any microphones. Till later on, later. I was playing in South Bend, Indiana. And a fellow came up to me and he said, man, he says, there's something coming out real soon that I sure would like to see you get on. And I'm going to try to help you. And it was television. When was that? This must have been about 33 or 34. It was in its infancy.
Yeah.

Yeah. And this guy, he could foretell that this was going to be a tremendous deal. And he says, with that band you have here, it'd be tremendous. But it never, to me, went in one hand and came out the other. Because to me, the guy was just talking out of his hat to be talking. Which a lot of times people do. But this time, it was actually something to listen to.

Well, I remember, I think it was 39, I saw television at the World's Fair in New York. And I didn't think anything about it. I thought, you know, as a kid, this is just another scientific wonder and you don't pay much attention to.
Well, that's just how to do it. With a grain of salt.
So, you know, nothing's ever going to happen to it. It's very interesting and all that. But, well, I don't think I even understood it at that age.
No, no, no. About 12 years old. Well, that's right.
I didn't have any idea what, well, nobody understood what the future was on.
Right, well, how could you go that far in the advanced days there?
No.

Well, of course, now all of my music life wasn't beautiful, I'll say. We really ran into some grave problems. I think I talked to you about some of these incidents a couple of times before. Being as light as I was, they considered me a white musician. Then when they found out that I was actually a Negro, then it changed the whole picture. Traveling with the wives in the bands, you ran into problems there with the police, thinking that they were prostitutes or something like that. And there was always some incidents coming up to put a block into your happiness, I'd say. But, of course, we always managed to smile at it after it was over with. And we were stranded a lot of times on the highways with nothing to eat, nothing to drink. And fortune would shine on us, somebody would come along and help us out. So we made it through the storm a lot of times that way.
You got stranded with no money, no nothing?

Right, right. Right. Right. Right. When we had this big trouble in Thomasville, Georgia, and I wanted to lynch the whole band, it took all of the money. We had made $150 that night, which was a lot of money for my band. Well, they took every dime we had. And got ready to get the gas to go to Macon, Georgia, which was 150 miles. The attendant was a good enough man to give me enough gas and trust me with gas and oil to get to Macon, Georgia. Then I sent him his money for Macon as soon as I got there. I knew the doctor that was promoting the dancing. I wanted him his money right back. That's one of the many, many instances where you say everybody in this world is not bad. And you can't say that every white man is bad because it's a lie. You can't say every Negro is bad. It's a lie because everybody is not. Now this one particular fella, supposing he hadn't come to our aid, he'd probably been in the neck and jaw, I mean, in the east of the town of Thomasville, Georgia, dead now. And then of course the problems of eating on the highway, sleeping, and those accommodations, which today, like I explained in one of my talks to one of these singers at the Sabarell Center, I don't remember, I don't think you'll recall that television shot I made over here. They were playing here at the Brewer Room and I told a lady, I said, you could sit here and smile and enjoy what you're doing today. I said, it's beautiful. I said, but let me tell you some of the experiences that I've had to make it possible for you to enjoy this life today and see how hard it was. But these today, they don't know it. They don't know anything about the past. They're not looking for the past. They're looking for the present. And that's what it is. But I do think that history should be there and someone with a vivid idea and a memory of what happened in the early 20s, and the early 30s, would document this and document it correctly and don't pull any punches. Maybe out of a hundred, maybe ten might read it. But that is a fact there before your eyes would actually happen.

If you don't have any history and you don't have any tradition, then you're along with stuff. You know, they give you some sort of guide to how to behave. Well, of course, kids think they know it all. Anyhow, let me know if you want any coffee or anything.
Well, no, I'd rather finish this than drink to call it.
Okay. How many numbers did you have that would feature just one man in your big band?
You mean as a solo? All the numbers featured some artists, one of the fellas in the band.
There may be several or it may be just one. Yeah, sure.
So for instance, there never was one individual that stood out and the whole number built around him. It was a band. And it featured everyone in the band that could play.

But you go to, you used to go to Louis Armstrong concerts, say in the 50s and the 60s. And he would then, he'd have one number, like he'd have a program built in such a way that he'd feature Buster Bailey on Memphis Blue. But that was a later thing. You never had a star deal.

Yeah, but here's the difference here. There was only five or six pieces there. Mine, I had 14. So you couldn't combine it to one individual. But five piece bands, yes, that's how they had to operate. Well, for instance, the concert last night, it would have been lost if you couldn't feature each individual.
Yeah, that's right.
But by being able to feature each individual, it spreads your program over a period of time, which you're looking forward to. And also giving this guy the credit that's doing.
Yeah. Yesterday afternoon, I thought you. Which reminds me of something. I never had figured out where Cottrell got his tenor saxophone style. Maybe I just don't know enough about tenor saxophone.
Well, Cottrell was the tenor player in the band.
Yeah. Featured, huh?

Right. See, we had the clarinet wasn't a popular instrument in those days. It was the saxophones, the altos and the tenor. And of course, Hall doubled on the baritone. He got to sound like Duke's band. But on the feature, sometimes maybe Cottrell wanted to get away from his tunning, such as on the sheet of the band, even in the feature of his clarinet, which was a great thing.
But he did play tenor solo all of a sudden?
Sure. Great tenor player.
Well, I think so. And, you know, most guys sound like Hawkins to me, you know.
No, Cottrell had his own style. Beautiful. Beautiful, great tone.
Yeah, and I don't think he was just an imitator of anybody.
In fact, I didn't have an imitator in the band. Or they played some solo in the vein of the other fella. Sure they did. Everybody copies somebody somewhere. Yeah, but it's still, uh...

Well, it's still not, uh, note for note sitting around an hour and night long like some people out here nowadays. It's playing a series of riffs, it's the same thing. Just juggling riffs around that they picked out from somebody else. Well, what about Geechee Fields? Who do you think he sounded like?

You mean Geechee Robison? I mean Geechee Robison. I'm trying to write. That's a New York drama pop. I'm trying to write at the same time. Yeah, but here's the thing about Geechee. Geechee didn't have a set style. He didn't copy anyone, but he did try to play solos in Tricky Sam style with Dewey. But he also played his own solos.
Yeah, well if anything, you know, to me it sounds like he listened to maybe a Jimmy Harrison song.
Very little.
Very little like him. Maybe he listened to Armstrong?
More like Tricky Sam.
Yeah, but on the record, you know, you don't hear that. No. That's funny. The Tricky Sam part doesn't come through.
Look at this, uh, plunger.
Yeah. Well that, that, that isn't on the record.
No, no, he didn't. He didn't. I recall now. He didn't use it on that.
Yeah, and so I was wondering if you'd listen to Jimmy Harrison, or Sandy Williams, or Louis Armstrong. To me, Armstrong affected a lot of trombone players, yeah.
Yeah. Affected every musician that plays.
Every drummer, the drummer players, everything. Yeah, everybody.

Yeah. Yeah. Somewhere or another, somewhere in his playing, he's gonna do something to remind you of Louis. Which I think is the greatest thing in the world as a memorial to a man. Or, say for instance, at the, at the concert yesterday when I dedicated the, the second half of my program to the memory of Louis. I tried to play some of his numbers that really are all outstanding recordings. When you're smiling. And, Hello Dolly, which was his last big one.
Yeah.
And that way, while you're not taking away, you're just adding to the, to the fella's life.

Oh, when the band was built on posters and then advertisements in the newspapers and stuff like that. I think we talked about this before. Do you have any of those posters or ads to show how to build?

I sure wish I did. Danny Balka asked me that question here. Yeah. And, of course, here's what happens. When you're young, you're going great, you don't think of what's gonna happen in the future. Mm-hmm. I should have said, well I have quite a number of old write-ups that have faded that you barely can read.
You ought to get those Xerox. That's the thing. Take them down.

I don't believe you could even Xerox and there's so much on it that, maybe I might send you one of these books and you can pick out what you think could be Xerox. You can pick out these Xerox at your convenience and at your time.
Yeah, I might find somebody who could do it in some sort of special way.

Maybe so. But, I have a few of them. And then too, a lot of this stuff was stolen from me. The Booking Age, it's like Al Travis, the biggest crook in the world. Then comes Rabinowitz, another Jewish Booking Age. And this guy, Chauncey Hallin. These guys take my material and when they jump the gun, I never see them on my material and all that's gone. Which was a big loss to me. Pictures, stories, and things like that.
Well, I guess sometimes you'd get top billing and sometimes you wouldn't. Well, yeah. It was very.

Top billing and most of the time in the cities but on the stages might have been a review. So, you're just another part of the review. So, for instance, this is Ralph Cooper's review. Mm-hmm. Featuring Don Albert's Big Bang. Who was Ralph Cooper? Ralph Cooper was a producer in New York. Mm-hmm. He was just like Larry Steele and those guys who don't know anything about him. I only heard their name. But they were producers. He produced the show at the Fowlers in Brooklyn. That's where Ella and all these other upcoming stars. We had a big production. Mm-hmm. And Glens Falls, New York. We had Billy Holiday up in Glens Falls, New York. And the buildings, everyone would, Ralph Cooper would be the headliner. Yeah. So, so, so, so, so.
Yeah, well, that's more honest than the way they do things now sometimes. I don't know.
Well, today, if you don't give a man Todd Billing, he might walk out on you.

Yeah. Well, I mean, sometimes you need to know who the producer of a show is. Because they, guys, they had certain reputations. Right. And some producers had integrity and some of them didn't. Some guys, you know, it seemed to me that they're good producers. They deserve a lot of credit. Right. People don't realize that. Just like a lot of people don't think a band leader does anything. They don't know what he does after the show is open, before it goes on.
They don't know what he does when the others are sleeping. Yeah. And in my case, I had to do the leader, trumpet player, booking agent, and father and mother to the band. Mm-hmm.
Yeah, you had to do everything.
You know something I noticed?
I was listening to Boots' Callous Love. And he even got sort of a Dixieland sound.
Boots was, to me, a Dixieland drummer.
Yeah.
Yeah. The only thing, he wasn't from New Orleans. Yeah. The guy had a real Dixieland beat. Good beat. Good drummer. Good cymbal man.
Yeah, I was impressed with that, that a guy would have that kind of Dixieland flavor to his plan.
That's right. Yeah, some good musicians in the band, I feel, they could easily sit in the Dixieland band and play it.
Whereas your band, unless I knew you were from New Orleans, I would not necessarily have spotted it, maybe Contrell, you know, because you didn't, on the record I'm talking about, you know.

Yeah, that wasn't later, that's after the big arrangements came up. Yes. But at the first plane, which we don't have any records of, in 1929 at the State Fair, nine musicians from New Orleans, you didn't have anything but a New Orleans beat. Yeah. Everybody was from New Orleans, except for one man, Hiram Hardy.
But even so, you were...
But those records are not captured in those days. Yeah, all that stuff. The ones that are captured now, in the later years, when the arrangements and the style of the band had changed.
You had to change the style of the band, yeah. Yeah.

But there was always that, they said, there's something about this band that makes you want to dance. Well, I've got to give credit to Fats Martin. Now, if you close the curtain in front of Freddie Coleman, and close your eyes, you'd hear Fats Martin. It's almost identical. Fats Martin was the greatest drumming that I've ever heard. And he set the tempos. And it was something, now and then a fast number, which people would try to dance on, but they couldn't. It was mostly a feature number that featured musicians.

What about, I can't remember if I've answered this before. People in New Orleans have another language, I mean, not just the Creoles, but the whole, they picked up a lot of French and Spanish things here. What about in Texas? Do they say any of the same words over there? What do they say?
You mean in the pronouncing of your English words?
No, no, I mean just different, entirely different words. Does anybody ever say Bank it in Texas? You'd never hear that.

No, you never hear those old slangs from down here. You never do. I understand what you mean, Bank it, and what's meant side walk. No. Because when we first went there, we had the little brogue that we brought with us later on. By associating with other people, we lost it. But we used to say those old words like tree and ting, and Dr. Tidge, you know. Yeah. Yeah, all things like that. But it got away from us, just like my French. I can talk French, yeah, but not fluently like I did when I was a boy, because my grandmother talked to me nothing but French, and so did my grandfather. But the English over there was altogether different. No funny words like we used in La.
No lanyard?

No lanyard. No, they don't know what the hell, what that is. No, no second line? No, no, no, no. You didn't read the little article about the second line. I was telling Segura yesterday that people are alike all over. And I met up with Buddy Tate up in New York, and I was on one of my visits up there. And Milton Larkins, and I said, man, let's march these cats around the place. He said, man, they don't know nothing about that up here. Yeah. I said, okay, watch me. Yeah. So I got to playing, and I dug a cat in the audience and said, look like he was really enjoying what we were playing. I said, come on, man. I said, follow me. And I thought, first thing you know, we had the whole house walking all up and down 7th Street and back up the steps. Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm .
The third reel of Don Albert, September 18, 1972. We were talking about Buddy Tate, you were up there in New York. You were sitting in or something and you guys started dancing?

No, I was on vacation and Buddy was playing at the Celebrity Club and Nathan Larkins was upstairs and so we just all got together, reunion or sort of, and we just started jamming up there and blowing. And these cats marched just like they do down here. And that's what the write up says in the paper this morning about the concert yesterday. How they marched in the aisles. It seems that it looks like it's only my programs here that really jumped up and down like I had them yesterday.
Well, I think it was very successful.
Well, I think it was successful both ways, financial and pleasing to the public too. As God, the comments are still coming in.

Well, I was sitting with people that knew about music and some of them anyway, certainly, and they appreciated a good lead on it, a good MC, and that's part of what Buddy Tateau. Back to the words and the way they're used here in New Orleans. If you say something is terrible in Texas, what does that mean?
It means it's bad. That's not one of the words of Ron Hill. Terrible is a nationally used word.

Yeah, but I mean, people in New Orleans sometimes will say, oh, he's a terrible trumpet player. They mean he's great. Right. Oh, he's a bad trumpet player. Yeah, well, that's the slang. Yeah, do they use that in Texas? They say that same thing, don't you? Yeah, sure they do. I thought that was true.
And some guys say, man, he's crazy. It means the guy's good. It's just slang word.
Well, Lester claims to have started a lot of that stuff.
Lester Young? Yeah. Well, the man that started most of it was Lloyd. Lloyd had a lot of slang words.
Oh, yeah. What about Carnival? Did they have anything at all like Carnival?

There was something similar to what we do here, but not on a big scale in Galveston years ago. They had tried it. Well, there was a lot of Louisiana people that migrated into Galveston through Beaumont, Texas, and they tried to do the things there that was done in New Orleans, but the people in Texas wasn't ready for it.
Well, I always found Galveston is more like New Orleans than any other Texas town somewhere around.
In a way of the living, yeah. Well, that's because you had a migration there from Louisiana through Port Arthur and Beaumont.
There was something else that was going on here. I'll tell you about that. Well, what was Carnival like when you were growing up? Did we talk about that, about the different clubs and things?

Well, here in New Orleans? Here in New Orleans. I saw it when I was a barber. Yeah. Or something like that. Well, it always was a big day that we looked forward to. But as I've said before, it's changed so considerably from the old days. The old days, I imagine, there wasn't quite as many people as it is now because, man, this thing is mushroomed to an extent where you wonder where these people are going to actually go. And in the old days, there weren't so many, but a lot of masques. They had their own outfits and things like that, the music. And now it's commercialized. And in those days it was just a fun day. And you know what I'm talking about when I say commercialized.
Oh yeah. But you had little, what do you want to call them, clubs, bands?

Clubs and groups would get together. Yeah. What were some of the groups then? Well, neighborhood groups. They would mask like, imitate something in the storybook like a skeleton or a bear, something like this. A bunch of kids would get together in the neighborhood. And they'd go out in groups.
But they wouldn't have a name necessarily? Like a zulu?
Not necessarily. Well, no. You see, those are a few big organizations that had. You couldn't have, all these couldn't be clubs. It would have to just be a community thing.
Yeah. Well, I'm trying to think of some of the societies that are big.

Well, you had the Fros Amis for one. Yeah. But they didn't parade too much. Yeah. The Illinois club, was that downtown? That was downtown. That was the gentlemen's club. Mm-hmm. Oh, we used to play for that club. My big band. Illinois, I was a young man, 20. And well, you got quite a number of clubs like that, but not masking clubs. I see. But they would put on dances during the carnival season. Dances during the carnival season. Which they do yet. Yeah.
I wonder when the carnival season would start back then. Would you have any idea?
Same as it starts now. When it's- 12th, 9th, around. Right. Right. See, that's a tradition. Yeah. But now it's going back further and further. Well, that brings me back to the commercialism.

Yeah. Yeah. Well, that's why. In a way, it's a good thing, because it does keep- Some of these people could be- could stand to be kept on that toes. I mean, that thing looks so ratty, those floats and all that. Yeah. That's right. The commercial people sometimes do a better job than the people who are way up in society. What are some of the Texas holidays that you celebrate?

Well, they have a holiday down there. There used to be a holiday down there to Negroes. We used to celebrate it, which was the 19th of June. That's, in other words, it's a Freedom Day. Juneteenth. I heard of it. Juneteenth. I heard of it. They're fastly getting away from that. The young ones don't want to associate themselves with-
They don't want to celebrate Freedom. No. That's funny with all that talk about Freedom.
But they don't want that as an example to where the full patterns come from.
But what goes on on Juneteenth?

Not anything anymore, but in the old days, they used to gather and they'd have barbecue, soda water, beer, and a band. And it would last all day, starting tomorrow and then last on until 12.1.2. Probably 90.
What about the 4th of July? What would you do?
Well, the 4th of July, everybody celebrates it. And, of course, you have your Mexican population on there that celebrates the day, Seseis, September.
The what?

The day, Seseis, September, which means the 16th of September. That's their Freedom Day. Freedom from Mexico. And, of course, the other holidays are in there, the national holidays, Columbus Day and Thanksgiving.
Would you have a barbecue on the 4th of July?
Yeah, they have outdoor barbecues. Friends gather and families gather on their lawns and things like that and barbecue.
What about fireworks in Texas? When would you shoot the fireworks?
They'll still shoot them.
4th of July? Sure. Christmas?
They shoot them any time they feel like it. It's against the law, but they find a way to shoot them any hour.
Well, in New Orleans, it seems to me people shoot fireworks at Christmas and I'm trying to remember them.
Just a couple of days. Well, they'll shoot fireworks in Texas whenever they feel like shooting.

Yeah, it might be July the 1st or January the 1st. That's right. Just so you felt like shooting fireworks and shoot them off. I just wondered. It seems to me that different sections, they have different customs. I mean, 4th of July, certainly everywhere. Everywhere. But other days.

Well, those are the big things in there. And of course, the Mexican population also has another one, Cinco de Mayo. That's the 5th of May. Did you play for them? Oh, I played for a number of Mexican dances.
Yeah, but I mean for those days.
Yeah, sometimes we were.
How do they celebrate it? I mean, they must have, you say dancing? Food?
Yeah, the regular routine of any other thing you see around here. Band playing, dancing, singing, food and drinks. Of course, they had their fabulous costumes, if they were.
Oh, yeah.
The traditional Mexican costumes.
What did the Creole people do for Christmas? Where? Here in New Orleans.
I don't think there's anything special.
Nothing special. No special food or anything?

No, the only time you had a special food in New Orleans that I can remember is St. George's Day when the Italians used to dress the altars up in the house and you would go by and get your bread or something like that. That's the only time that I can remember any food being involved in a traditional day.
Well, I think of turkeys as being a Thanksgiving and Christmas.
Well, yes, sure. Of course, that's traditional, though. It's national. Yeah, that's national.
What about donuts? When are donuts served to visitors? Do you ever do that? Don't have any of that. I often thought of putting up a donut place in Texas.
No, I mean here in New Orleans. When did you serve donuts? Oh. Would that be a special day for donuts? Well, the Mardi Gras Day was the day they served beans and donuts.
Served beans? Red beans and rice. And donuts, yeah.

That's a traditional food for, well, here's what they do. They cook this food the day before. And the early morning, everybody would get ready to go on the street. And then you come to the house, you get your dinner or you go to a friend's house. And usually you had your donuts and your beans and rice and pickled meat, whatever they call it. Yeah. That was one of Louis's great dishes. And when I first had Louis as my guest in 1931 in Oklahoma City, I wired him and I told him that I'd have his favorite dish when he got there. And he couldn't wait to get to the house because Louis hadn't had any red beans in a long time. And I had gotten some from New Orleans.
Yeah, well, I get red bean hungry sometimes. I do too.
I love beans. I love them.
What about king cakes? Did you ever have king cakes?
Sure. I used to try to get the pecan out of it. Get the pecan, you'd get a king cake next week.
You mean if you got the pecan, then you were the...
You'd have to buy the king cake next week.
Did you, well, was this a club or what? No, no.
Just regular family. Oh, the family.
I see. You'd have a king cake at home. Right.

And it was every week. Well, it would finally wear out after maybe two or three weeks. That was the hand that I... But when the first one would come out, that's when everybody wanted to go rob a king cake and get that pecan.
And when is the first one served?
I don't remember the exact date on King's Day. It was only using on a Sunday. Yeah, I see. And then the following Sunday and then the following Sunday.
Usually it's around 12 and 9th or something like that.
Something like that if I were right, but I just can't remember.
But you wanted to buy the king cake.
Yeah.
That was a real honor.
That was an honor to buy the king cake. I see.
Did you have many humbugs on the job where you were playing? I mean like in the audience? Fights? Yeah, fights and stuff.

Not that I can ever recall. The dances started early and they cut out early. But I can't ever recall. There might have been some differences there, but not no major fights as I said before. I can't recall. And Texas was a little different. They did have places there where it was always a knockout drag out.
Oh, in Texas.

In Texas. When I first went to Dallas, there was a place where I played upstairs. They had a man on the door to search each customer to come up. They had a bucket there on the side to drop the knives and the pistols in until they come out. But I never recall seeing anything like that in New Orleans. And I'll play to some tremendous crowds here. At the old Santa Center Club when I played there. I remember 1500, man. In those days, 1500 is equal to 5,000, 6,000, 7,000, 8,000 a day. And I can't recall any arguments or fights. Of course, a lot of times the audience was confined to the bandstand watching the band play. And they would just hang around and leave when the dancers are out. No trouble. But today, you can't tell when trouble is going to happen. I've never witnessed too much of it here yet because I guess it's maybe because I don't live here and I don't get a chance to go to these things. But I do read in Louisiana, Rita, about a lot of murders and things that go on here that are not associated with entertainment.
Well, yeah. That can happen anywhere. Right. On the street. Right.
Just be walking home at night. That's right. Well, that's predominant over the United States today. Yeah. So it's not confined to one city only.
Were you ever afraid walking home at night in any neighborhood?

I'll tell you, the first time that I, when I left New Orleans and I went to Dallas, Texas, I was so happy to be going away from New Orleans on my, starting on my career. I was always loved my family. So I was going on to the Western Union, which was about four, six or seven blocks from where I was playing. I was on the main street to Dallas. And I had a brand new trumpet. So I went into the Western Union and I said, no mother, telegram. And told her everything was all right and this, that, and the other. So when I came out, the policeman stopped me and says, what do you got in that box? Well, I'm about 60 years old. And I'm used to the lights in New Orleans staying all night, traveling the streets all night. They surprised me. I said, well, I got a trumpet. He said, open it. Now what he was looking for, I don't know, but after going through all these different things, these different phases in my life, maybe he was looking for don't. So he said, what else you have? And I said, nothing. So I said, I'm a musician. I just finished playing. He said, well, you're in a bad neighborhood. You see? It's on the main street.
Main street.

It was only about six blocks from the place where I was playing, which was predominantly the Negro neighborhood. And they had this railroad track down there, as you recall, it was called Central Track. And that's where all the thugs lived. And I guess I was too younger to realize the danger. So he told me, you better get on home and get on home and run quickly, right quickly, because some of you niggas will take your head off. He thought I was a white boy. Yeah. So I said, okay, I thanked him so much, so I left and I went. But my situation was this. It looked like all of the bad characters in the time would take up with me. I mean, real bad, shady characters that everybody was afraid of. Yeah. And I imagine it helped me a lot because one time I was up in what they call North Dallas. And this fellow was always six, about six feet, five inches tall. They called him Black Mac. And boy, he was tough. I mean, tough. And so the fellow said, oh, oh, he said, oh, mess with that little fellow there. I said, that's that Creole from New Orleans. And that's Black Mac's close buddies. He said, if you mess with him, Black Mac will get you. Oh, young and, you know, like this, you just laugh at things like that. Yeah. Later on in years, you realize, well, hell, man, this was something on your side. And it looked like it was my fortune or my good fortune, even in New York, to meet up with these guys. They said, take a liking to me, you see. And, well, that's it. A good friendly association treated me like a king. Wouldn't let nobody call me or nothing else. What is a Creole, anyway? Well, no, that's a debatable subject. My wife loves to call herself a Creole. They call me a Creole. The way that I see it, it is a mixture of races. The Creole has everything. We have Indians, we have Filipinas, we have Turks. We have Italians, which you know my name. I told you, Dominic, you would have pirate on the ship. Come from the Dominican Republic, Gene Defeat. That's where this creation of color has come in to call you a Creole. Now, there have been some real dark, dark Creoles. They call them Creoles because they're from the original Creole family. And sometimes a family, it goes, you see a family that has three or four real light-complected ones. And you look again, you see a dark one, but he's still the full brother and sister. Well, I think that's a debatable item, and I don't like to dwell too much on it. Because I might say something that might offend somebody, which I would most certainly not want to do. But that's the only answer that I can give for him.
How long has it been since you've been on a streetcar?
Oh, my goodness. It has to be 60-some years.
And do you ever ride the buses today?
Never do. I don't ride the buses in San Antonio. I don't ride the buses here.
Do you really feel that you don't like the high day of the bus?

Maybe it was a disappointment in my young days when I used to have to get on the streetcar and take and move the screen back for me to get a seat. I've always been conscious of being what they call a Negro. And you're brought up to know that this is your place here and this is your place there. You don't go here and you don't go there. And as I got older and I started fighting for civil rights and things like that, then there's some things that irritate you that you don't want to be reminded of. So I stay away from places like the buses and the streetcars.
And Dutch, you tell me she had?

Oh, Dutch, she caught holy hell in her days because she's so light and she had yellow hair. But the Negroes didn't want to accept her. When the white people found out she was a Negro, they didn't want to accept her. So it's been a problem.

Well, you know, I saw her yesterday and it takes you aback when you see her. You know, it's hard for me to realize it looking at it from the standpoint of being white, that she's not white, you know, when you first see her.
Right. Well, that's been the problem she's had.
She must have really suffered.
Oh, we've suffered quite a lot.
But you can't give up your fight for something you believe in.

You don't. You don't give up. The only thing you give up, you have to give up to your age. See, when I was young, I could fight and fight and fight. But Ma, at 64 years old, man, the fight's almost gone.

Yeah. Well, you get tired. Oh, you have to get tired. You get tired. What were some of the big theaters here, by the way? Did you ever hear of the Elysian Theater? I used to go there. Well, that's a new one on the island.
The Elysian?
Yeah, I just heard of it once.

Used to be right down here off of the Frenchman and, is that the one you're talking about? One off of Frenchman's Creek? Yeah. Frenchman and Elysian Field? Somewhere around. That's why it was called Elysian. Yeah. And Elysian Field runs there. Of course, you had these theaters up here in town off Iberville Street, the old palace. Mm-hmm. And you had the Orpheum. Is that still going? The Orpheum?
Yeah. It's still going. But the palace is gone. It's not quite the same thing. But the palace is gone. The palace is gone.
And then there was the Negro Theatre, the Lyric.
Yeah.
Well, that was a melting pot for some of the great musicians. Mm-hmm. There was a left-hand violin player there. I can't recall his name. John Robichaud. No, no.
There's not a one.
Val Coo. Val Coo? Mr. Val Coo. I've heard of Val Toe. Val Toe. Yeah.
Val Toe. It's either Val Coo or Val Toe.
But then you also had these great drummers that like Red Happy. But he was an import. He wasn't originally from here.
Not originally from nowhere.

I think he came from Memphis. But this guy was a trick drummer. Oh yeah. And of course you had old man Cottrell that was strictly a drummer. He was a Finnish musician drummer. Of course my daddy knew these people and he was real close friends with them. And he used to tell me. And I met them and I knew them. They knew me real well. I was just a kid. But the friendship always is beautiful.
What about the View of Korea in those days at Bourbon Street and all that? When did Bourbon Street start booming? Do you remember?

No, I sure can't dig. There was nothing when you were a kid? No, sure you had a lot of these. That's where the, well as they say the Hattons was. Plus Storyville, which was the, where Lula White and all this was. Yeah. But the joints were still there because you can look at the old Absinthe House and see how old that thing is. Yeah. So that's part of it.
There were some joints anywhere in the Bourbon Street. Sure there were some joints.
In the old days the big thing though were the balls, the dances at the Franz Ami Hall. And each section there. And then you had this San Su uptown and different places like that. Mostly dances.
I got a million questions here.

Well I tell you what, if you don't finish those questions, you mail them in to me and I'll do just like I do with Dick Allen. I'll answer them against the question. Leave a space there. Yeah. So I can just write it in there. Yeah.
You mean like you do with Driggs? With Driggs?
Who did I say?
Dick Allen. What the hell am I?
Well you see, Driggs will ask a question. Yeah. And that leaves a space and I'll just answer them there.
Well, let me get my stuff together and you can just talk. I was going to ask you about things like hunting and crawfishing kind of here in the old days.

Well, I can recall when I used to go and meet my daddy at Lake Punching Train. I know you asked me just now was I ever afraid. I said no. I'd go through the woods. I'd go and meet him at Lake Punching Train and go fishing and come on. That's after I delivered my papers. Crawfish, I used to go catch them back at old Jordan Avenue Canal and be among the thousand snakes. And these old, they call them water mugs, these cotton mugs. And I'd go ahead and catch my crawfish and carry my sacks and my nets out and come on out and peddle them off. That was another means of making a few knickers to run the house.
Let me get my neck down and my coat to be ready to roll. Yeah, alright.
Yeah.
Did people go out to restaurants ever then and take a bus?
Not like it is now. Everybody cooked their own meals at the house and everybody was a good cook.
When was the first time you ever remember going out to a restaurant? Yeah.
I didn't quite hear that, Dick.
When was the first time you ever remember going out to a restaurant?

To eat dinner? Yeah. Well, I'll tell you what, Dick. I still am reluctant to go to cafeterias or cafes. I don't do too much of it now. I never did. I like to eat at home, but my wife and my daughter, every now and then they'll say, Daddy, let's go get something to eat at the Luby's or one of the other big restaurants in San Antonio. I said, I'll agree with them because that's what they like. But our president would stay away from them. It comes back to what I said before. When I was traveling, I could go in certain places. In fact, I could go in most of any place. But after I got in there, I was always under the impression that somebody was going to say that I was a Negro and I'd have to get out of that. So today, that fear, I imagine, is not a fear, but it's just something that hits you and says, Well, you're not going to be wanted in there. And even though sometimes the reception is beautiful, you still feel like the eyes are on you.
Yeah. It makes you uncomfortable.
Right. It makes you uncomfortable. Which it shouldn't be. No. Because it has changed tremendously. Yeah.
Well, it's funny.
Tremendously it has changed. And you shouldn't feel like that. But there are still some places that gives you that impression that you're not wanted there.
Well, you feel a draft. You feel a draft.
That's right.
You know, it's like one time I took a roll of Kirk's mom and he thought he was still in a draft. You know, you can't call a matron D, but you know what I mean. The head waitress.
The head waitress.

Yeah. She came out and wanted this autograph. You know. Yeah. So naturally he was getting really great treatment and I had this waiter that I needed. But you know, people let things, they build things up too much as well. You know. What kind of fellas were in there?
Roland Kirk. Roland Kirk. I've never met him. Oh, he's a very nice guy. Of course naturally being blonde he has certain feelings. Right, right. Well that was the same way with Al Hibbler.
You know, Al Hibbler and I were great friends and I heard Al Hibbler when he was a kid in Little Rock, Arkansas.

And he want to join my band and he had sung some numbers with me. He'd sung some numbers with me. I'd already had a singer, so I... Later years he came to San Antonio, I used him at my nightclub, and then he went to Jim, like Shannon's band from J-Bone, to Duke's band, which I think was great. Only bad feature about Al, him, has always been his drinking problem. Being blind, he thought that, you know, people couldn't tell that. I imagine that's how you felt, but you can always tell when you felt it's not right. Yeah. Small. But, he was a great singer. Beautiful. Well, Dick, you're going to go to school now, so anyhow, I'm going to call my boy up and have him come and get him. And in the meantime, save these write-ups for me, and when you write and ask the questions, just give me enough space. Yeah. Let's hurry up and get this book on the way, man.
