Well, we hope we got this publisher lined up in Texas. Well, I must have said that drinks that's a good book. Yeah. No, I just happened to, I wrote you, I met a guy from Texas and might have a whole series of books.
I don't drink so better now, I have one at the house to write.

Well, it's a shame to let all this material not get published, and yet it's hard to find anybody who's interested in it. Right, they're interested in it. And they publish, you know, really second-rate books and all of that. And certainly if anybody knows about Kansas City music and Texas and Oklahoma and all that is Frank Drake. And I think everybody in the business knows that.
Well, Frank Drake's got all of this information from me. Yeah.
But I mean, he's the one who's done the most writing. Right. And then, uh...
But he still hasn't gotten a book on it. And it's funny... There's still a lot of questions unanswered that I can't answer for him.
Yeah, there's a lot of questions, a lot of things that have to be traced out. But it's funny how he, I never have understood why he can't have found a publisher.
Well, the only way Drake's gonna get what he wants out of me is to come down and see me or I go up and see him, as I do what you said. Yeah. Just these questions on a piece of paper and I'll be...
No, that's not nearly as good. That's only a start. Hmm.
Well, it was nice meeting you, Dave.
Yeah. Okay, you can call him back and use the phone. I'll let this run off and I'll start packing stuff up now. Okay.

segments.title: Opening of reel 1, Sept 18, 1972
segments.summary: Interviewer states the date and location (910 Royal Street) at the start of the tape.

segments.title: Geechee Robinson's moon-driven mood changes
segments.summary: Albert describes bandsman Geechee Robinson, who turned Jekyll-and-Hyde and picked arguments at certain times of the month; he later went with Fletcher.

segments.title: Refined, well-behaved men in Albert's band
segments.summary: Compared with Lunsford's college men, Albert's band members were gentlemen, many schooled with Cottrell, and almost none drank.

segments.title: Stage acts: Alcorn on the lap and throwing instruments
segments.summary: Albert and Alcorn did a trick act, fingering each other's horns, and bands generally used showmanship motions.

segments.title: Growing up in the French Quarter among musicians, Danny Barker next door
segments.summary: Albert names the Creole neighbourhood and the musicians who lived there, including Bigard, Manuel Perez, Piron, and Danny Barker across the street.

segments.title: Peddling charcoal and illegal shrimp with Danny's father
segments.summary: He and Danny helped Chris Columbo peddle coal and wood by wagon; other peddlers sold shrimp illegally.

segments.title: Obedient kids then versus today
segments.summary: Albert recalls playing in neighbours' yards, being disciplined by any elder, and argues youth are harder to control now.

segments.title: Affectionate Creole families and the family concert
segments.summary: Creoles hug and kiss when they meet; Albert's sister sold over 200 concert tickets.

segments.title: Homemade balls and boyhood odd jobs
segments.summary: Kids made balls from stockings and earned nickels shining faucets, shopping and shining shoes.

segments.title: Stickball, Crescent Stars Park and the Negro league players
segments.summary: Ball games on the greens and the old Crescent Stars Park, with pitcher Joe Perdo, Satchel Paige and Josh Gibson.

segments.title: Caffery Darensbourg, Piron and the Autocrat Club symphony men
segments.summary: Albert praises genius mandolinist Caffery Darensbourg, the Tios and teacher Armand Piron, and recalls singing at Autocrat Club Sundays.

segments.title: Satchel Paige's age and self-taught guitarists
segments.summary: Albert and Satch palled around in Dallas; talk turns to untaught players who still make the right changes.

segments.title: What makes a musician great, and reading with Troy Floyd
segments.summary: Willis Santiago and Caffery Darensbourg as all-round greats; Albert mostly read parts in Troy Floyd's band.

segments.title: Training around Perez, Piron and Moret; bass tone
segments.summary: Learning among the old masters, Jimmy Johnson's bass tone, Blanton and the importance of round tone.

segments.title: Frank Driggs's different version of stories
segments.summary: Albert wonders what Driggs meant about a different version of events, possibly from Texas.

segments.title: Hopscotch, hide and seek, and silent movie theater pits
segments.summary: Children's games and silent films with a pit pianist; Albert played in a theater pit with bassist Tolles as a kid; tape runs out.

segments.title: New Orleans without a wrong side of the tracks
segments.summary: Reel 2 begins with movie pianists, then neighbourhoods had no railroad-avenue divide and people rented homes.

segments.title: Killer-dillers and riff numbers
segments.summary: A killer diller was the number everyone could blow on, closing a set; riffs behind solos.

segments.title: Riff bands of the era, Troy Floyd and C.G. Conn instruments
segments.summary: Blue Devils, Basie, Lunceford, Trent and Troy Floyd's Orchestra of Gold; Conn supplied Albert's trumpets.

segments.title: Albert's tunes, Sheik of Araby and 'Alita'
segments.summary: Which numbers survive, his unpaid composition 'Truth', riffing on Sheik of Araby, and his own songs.

segments.title: Improvising over chord changes and chromatics
segments.summary: How soloists stay in the chord form, chromatic scales versus chromatics, and Barney Bigard's rating.

segments.title: French method books and Solfege
segments.summary: His stolen Clodomir method and solfege books, and what music is.

segments.title: 'Sunny Side of the Street' and Lloyd Glenn's piano interlude
segments.summary: Billy Douglas sang and played on the record; the piano interlude was Lloyd Glenn's written idea.

segments.title: Daily rehearsals on the road
segments.summary: The band rehearsed nearly every day, with no lateness or grumbling.

segments.title: Megaphones and an early television tip in South Bend
segments.summary: No microphones, only megaphones; a stranger in South Bend foretold television around 1933-34.

segments.chapter: Touring and race on the road
segments.title: Stranded on the road and the Thomasville, Georgia trouble
segments.summary: Passing for white, wives mistaken for prostitutes, and robbery in Thomasville where a gas attendant trusted him.

segments.title: Featuring every man in a fourteen-piece band
segments.summary: No single star; all numbers featured band members, unlike small bands.

segments.title: Cottrell's tenor style and the band's saxophones
segments.summary: Louis Cottrell was the tenor soloist with his own tone; Hall doubled baritone.

segments.title: Geechee Robinson's trombone style and Louis Armstrong's influence
segments.summary: Geechee played Tricky Sam style but his own solos; Armstrong influenced everyone and Albert dedicated his concert set to Louis.

segments.title: Lost posters, stolen material and Ralph Cooper's revue
segments.summary: Faded write-ups, crooked booking agents, and the Ralph Cooper revue; Albert was leader, trumpeter, agent and father to the band.

segments.title: Boots's Dixieland drumming and Fats Martin
segments.summary: The 1929 State Fair band had a New Orleans beat; Fats Martin set the tempos.

segments.title: Texas versus New Orleans words and a second line in New York
segments.summary: Texans lack New Orleans slang; Albert led a second line with Buddy Tate and Milton Larkins in New York.

segments.title: Reel 3: the Celebrity Club jam and New Orleans slang
segments.summary: The Buddy Tate Celebrity Club reunion, the concert's success, and slang like terrible meaning good.

segments.title: Carnival in Galveston and in New Orleans
segments.summary: Galveston's Carnival attempt, old neighbourhood masking, social clubs and dances during the season.

segments.title: Juneteenth, Fourth of July and Mexican holidays in Texas
segments.summary: Texas holidays: Juneteenth barbecues, fireworks, Sixteenth of September and Cinco de Mayo dances.

segments.title: Christmas, Mardi Gras beans and donuts, king cakes
segments.summary: New Orleans food customs, red beans for Louis Armstrong in 1931, and buying the king cake.

segments.title: Fights at dances, and a policeman in Dallas
segments.summary: Few fights at New Orleans dances versus knife-checking in Dallas; a Dallas policeman stopped Albert with his trumpet.

segments.title: Black Mac's protection and what a Creole is
segments.summary: Dallas toughs took to Albert as Black Mac's buddy; he defines Creole as a mixture of races.

segments.title: Avoiding streetcars, buses and the colour line
segments.summary: Streetcar segregation memories, his wife's hardships for being light-skinned, and tiredness at 64.

segments.title: Theaters, the Lyric and the old dance halls
segments.summary: Elysian, Palace, Orpheum and the Lyric with its musicians, plus Storyville and the dances.

segments.title: Mailing questions back, as with Driggs
segments.summary: Albert offers to answer leftover questions in writing.

segments.title: Crawfishing and fishing in boyhood
segments.summary: He caught crawfish in the canal and fished at Lake Pontchartrain, selling them; people cooked at home.

segments.title: Fear of restaurants and being unwanted
segments.summary: Albert still feels uneasy in restaurants; Roland Kirk anecdote.

segments.title: Al Hibbler friendship and drinking
segments.summary: Albert knew Hibbler as a Little Rock kid, used him in San Antonio; his drinking was the flaw.

segments.title: Book plans, Driggs and closing
segments.summary: Talk of a publisher for his book, Frank Driggs's research, and packing up.
